paras: The Phoenix cowboy fight and attempted lynching took place on August 2, 1882, in Phoenix, Arizona Territory, when city marshal Henry Garfias and a posse fought three mounted men described as cowboys, killing one, and a crowd then tried to hang the captured survivors on the way to jail. Officers with a posse rescued the prisoners, who were later discharged by a justice court and fined $100. The wire story ran in papers from Savannah to Nevada as a near escape from lynching, while the local Phoenix Herald praised the marshal and warned that future captives might not reach jail.

In the weeks before the fight the Phoenix Herald complained of a growing 'hoodlum, bummer and desperado element' in the town's saloons. The paper recalled that three years earlier Phoenix had found it 'necessary to hang two of them by lynch law.' The two captured men were later identified as William and Frank Lyle, brothers of Ned Lyle, whom the Herald described as captured by Sheriff Paul's posse near Calabasas a few days before.

According to the Herald, three riders careered through the back streets firing pistols, then rode on the sidewalks and into saloons on the main street, pulling pistols on citizens and shooting into private houses. Garfias called a posse of W. O. O'Neill, Manuel Garcia and H. McDonald, and when the riders charged, the leading man fired and a shot from Garfias broke his right hand. In the running fight that followed, one rider fell from his horse on Monroe street, shot through the head and lungs, and died soon after; the Herald named him as William Hardy. The other two abandoned their horses, took to the brush and were captured.

A special dispatch from Phoenix, relayed through Tucson and San Francisco, reported that as the prisoners were being taken through the town 'an attempt was made to lynch them.' They were pushed under a tree while loud calls were made for a rope, until officers with a posse came to the rescue and took them to jail, in one version 'for safety.' The Herald's own account of the fight says only that the two were 'marched up and lodged in jail', but a week later it claimed that during the excitement one of the defense lawyers had run through the streets shouting 'Hang them'.

The Lyle brothers had a preliminary examination before Judge Richards, with Judge Lemon prosecuting and A. C. Baker defending. Four men swore that the cowboys had shot at them, while defense witnesses swore they had not seen the defendants shoot. Richards discharged the brothers on the complaint and ordered them held on a misdemeanor charge, and the city court then released them with a $100 fine.

Governor Tritle, passing through Phoenix, endorsed the citizens' action, and a deputation headed by N. Rosenthal presented Garfias with a check from contributing citizens. No report of an inquest into Hardy's death, or of action against anyone in the crowd, appears in the coverage.

Outside Arizona the story spread as a short wire item on August 4, under headlines such as 'Saved from the Halter' in the Savannah Morning News, 'An Attempt at Lynching' in the Washington National Republican and 'Arizona's Lively Cowboys' in the Richmond Dispatch. Versions differed on details: the Savannah paper counted two cowboys rather than three, a Midwestern roundup placed the dead and wounded among the officers and citizens, and the Bolivar Bulletin moved the fight to 'Phoenix, Cal.' The Kenosha Telegraph summed up that the cowboys 'narrowly escaped lynching at the hands of the populace.'

The Phoenix Herald covered the fight under alliterative headlines such as 'City Cemetery Contains a Cow-Boy's Cussed Carcass' and called Garfias 'our brave Marshal.' Its editorials told the men's sympathizers that 'the sooner they make themselves scarce, the better,' and said that if the authorities failed, 'the citizens themselves will take care of it.' After the court's ruling the Herald attacked the decision and warned that next time 'the criminals, when captured, will never reach the safe quarters of the county jail.' The Tombstone Independent, quoted by the Herald, called the Phoenix papers 'fairly lurid' in their account.
None of the coverage gives the race of the men involved or frames the episode in racial terms.

The wire reports agreed that one man was killed and one badly wounded with 'No one else' hurt, but the Kenosha Telegraph and True Northerner reported that the dead and wounded were among the officers and citizens. The local Herald, which named the dead man as the cowboy William Hardy and said no townsman was hurt, is the stronger evidence on this point. Dispatches dated August 3 placed the fight 'last evening', while the Star special dated August 2 said 'this afternoon' and the Herald spoke of 'broad, open daylight' on Wednesday.

reader.title: Phoenix cowboy fight and attempted lynching
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: The wire reports describe an attempt by a crowd to hang two or three captured men on the way to jail, stopped by officers (A2, A4, A7); the one death came earlier, when the marshal's posse shot a man in the fight (A11, A12).

No one was killed by the crowd: the prisoners were rescued and jailed and later tried (A2, A23), and William Hardy died of wounds from the marshal's posse during an arrest (A11, A12). The crowd's attempt was an unlawful attempted lynching of men accused of shooting up the town (A4, A27).

The Tucson/Phoenix wire (A2, A4, A7) and the local Phoenix Herald (A11, A12, A24) independently agree on the fight, one man killed and the capture and jailing of the others; the attempted lynching rests on the wire and the Herald's later remark about calls to 'Hang them' (A24).

framing.detail: Eastern and southern dailies ran the wire under heads such as 'Saved from the Halter', 'An Attempt at Lynching' and 'Arizona's Lively Cowboys'.

The Phoenix Herald praised Garfias, recalled hanging two 'hoodlums' by lynch law three years earlier, told sympathizers to leave and warned that future captives might 'never reach the safe quarters of the county jail'.
Weekly news summaries compressed the story to one or two sentences, some misplacing it in California.

conflicts.note: The Herald's 'Wednesday' and 'two days ago' (A10, A13) support August 2 for the fight; the Evening Star's 'yesterday' likely reflects its Aug. 3 dateline.
